article_text:
Tate Modern presents the UK’s first ever solo exhibition of the work of Algerian artist Baya (Mahieddine). Featuring more than 100 of her vivid gouache watercolours, alongside unique ceramic sculptures, this show traces Baya’s groundbreaking impact across cultural landscapes in North Africa and Europe during the 20th century.

Forging an artistic and cultural identity in newly independent Algeria, Baya’s geometric patterns and bold colours were rooted in the creative and natural surroundings of her homeland, as well as its storytelling and musical traditions. Throughout her life, she defied attempts to categorise her work in terms like ‘surrealist’ or ‘naive’, instead claiming her distinctly modernist approach as simply ‘Baya-ism’.

Baya’s work has been influential on generations of international artists and thinkers, including figures such as Pablo Picasso and André Breton. This exhibition shines a spotlight on her practice, showcasing her extraordinary work on its own terms. It builds on new research to explore the complexity and experimentation at the heart of this hugely significant artist’s career.

Baya is presented in the George Economou gallery. Supported by Art Mentor Foundation Lucerne. With additional support from Tate Members.

After more than a decade out of the limelight and away from his wardrobe of high-visibility, low-practicality clothing, Sacha Baron Cohen ‘s Ali G is back with his first film in almost 25 years. This time, alongside the satirical would-be bad boy himself leading “Ali G: Who Iz I” comes his long-suffering girlfriend Julie (constantly referred to by Ali as “Me Julie”).

Played by British comic and impressionist Morgana Robinson, Julie is seen in the trailer to the film — released Oct. 23 by Amazon MGM — heavily pregnant while Ali first explains to a doctor that her bump is “probably wind or a big poo” and later with him as, when asked what type of father he wants to be, he replies “absent.”

For Robinson, who played Pippa Middleton in “The Windsors,” the experience making “Ali G: Who Iz I” was the most insane she’s ever had, one that required her, on the insistence of Cohen, to stay in character off set. “He was training me like Rocky,” she says. But for all the silliness of the film (Morgana claims it’s half-silly — ”laugh-out loud funny, but with a message”), “Ali G: Who Iz I” has also come under significant fire, accused of using outdated racist stereotypes and mocking the working class. In the U.K., there have also been calls for cinemas to boycott the film.

Speaking to Variety , a wildly entertaining Morgana claims that Julie — who she describes as “the heart of the film” — is much more than what’s been seen in the trailer, adding that the “Who Iz I” actually takes aim at Ali G’s out-of-date views and attitude. But she also laughs about the shock and surprise of finding people in America who didn’t know Ali G and could be duped by the joke and reveals the real — and painful — struggles of trying not to laugh during each scene, because “there is no take two.”

I’m in a bowl of jelly, to be honest. It is a bit knee-knocky. It’s on a rather grand scale, but it’s been amazing, especially on the red carpet and turning up in character.

I find it a bit of a comfort. It’s like a very solid bra. I feel supported and not so exposed. They can look a bit serious, can’t they? And if you look a bit silly, it’s fine.

It’s half-silly. It gets less silly as you go on. But it’s got all the feels. It’s outrageous. It’s very funny. It’s terrifying. It’s uncomfortable. It’s heartbreaking. It’s confusing. But it’s laugh out loud funny, but with a message.

He hasn’t changed particularly much, apart from you know his beard’s a bit longer. But how does he sit into today’s society? I think that’s sort of the reason they made this —what happens when you take a very dated character and drop him in into today’s society, into the world that we live in today that’s a very different place.

I might let you wait and see. But what I will say is that I think a lot of questions have been asked, and I think they get answers.

There was a very rigorous, full-on casting situation, and there were waves of auditions. There was like the first wave of auditions was a sort of like, “Hi, can you come in and have an improv with Sasha? Can you be funny? Can you go toe to toe with him? Can you hold your own?” And then the second, once you’ve passed that, was, “We throw you into the jaws of a shark with a with a real interview with a real person. Can you be believable?” I guess what they were looking for was a balance between someone who could be funny, but also someone who you know could feel real. Otherwise, I guess they don’t have a film. But I think it took them about a year to cast.

Oh yeah, I like the word ‘clandestine.’ It’s an odd it’s an odd fish, isn’t it? I mean, I’ve never done anything like this with real people. It was was crazy. Sometimes we were in the desert in Palm Springs. We stayed in these random hotels, all of us, but no one knew what we were doing there. So it was all sort of cloak and dagger and lying about what we were doing. You’d be doing makeup in your hotel room, and some days I’d come back and I’d have a bob and I’d be not pregnant. Then the next morning, I’d be eight months pregnant, walking out the lobby. Then I’d be in the bar having a glass of wine. And the concierge was just so confused.

Every single person, apart from me and him and the guy who plays his dad, are all real people. It think Borat is well known in America, but Ali G isn’t. But I think the people on the team scouted for people, and they had to pass a sort of certain test of who they know and what they know.

The whole thing is ridiculous. The whole thing is shocking and surprising. I don’t know where to begin. But the script was a constantly evolving thing. It wasn’t like, “Here is the script. You may read it.” It was like, “Here it is and it’s different from yesterday.” So you’re in your room waiting to come on set and 10 minutes before someone runs in going, “Hey Morgana, this has totally changed.” You’re like, “This is chaos. This is ludicrous. They’re never going to believe this. We can’t pull this off. This is impossible.” And I don’t know what happens, but [Cohen] sort of hypnotizes people. it’s like a magic trick.

There’s no take two. So that actually stops you from laughing a lot of the time. I did corpse twice in the entirety of filming. One was when I had to peel a banana with my toes, and the other one was something that happens later, but I don’t want to spoil it. So I did it twice, but I sort of managed to look away and stifle it. I bit so hard on my cheek. That’s one way of doing it. You can sometimes turn it into a cough. Or it can come out as a sort of twitch. But yes, it’s very hard.

He will not let you break character. So we’re in character for eight hours. It’s exhausting. Normally, when you’re acting, you’re like, that was a very big take, is it lunch break? But here you’re eating lunch in character or whatever you’re doing because they’re watching. It’s wild. I remember when we first started filming, I hadn’t seen Sasha since the audition and I got to the lot to do the first rehearsals and talk and read the script. I was like, “Oh, hi Sasha, it’s Morgana, I haven’t seen you for six months.” And he’s like, “In character! All day I want you in character! I never want to hear you speaking as Morgana! It’s always me Julie!” Then he’d march me down to the mall and be like, “Go and have an argument with some people and buy some socks and then come back and then call up your mother and have a conversation as me Julie and eat that bento box as me Julie. How would she use chopsticks?” He’s mad.

He was training me like Rocky. All day long, running up and down those steps, all sweaty.

I think I lost my marbles a little bit for a while, but I think I found them again. I think it’s sort of like sort of slow release PTSD. I can’t believe we fucking did that. I cannot believe that. I mean.. so I get kidnapped.

Yeah, I get kidnapped. That’s an actual thing. That’s not even the bad bit. That’s just in the second act. I get kidnapped. But more happens.

I get my minge out. You’ll probably have to change that because no one knows what a minge is in America. So all these years, I’ve been doing these cute little cult things, like Vic and Bob, and no one’s watched it. Really, all you need to do is just go to Hollywood and get your fanny out. You know, I’m 44. I’ve got to pay the mortgage.

Yes, indeed.

No, they’re not politicians. Not in my scenes anyway.

I found it difficult. So I just stopped reading them entirely. People have their opinions, and that’s absolutely fine. I am a character actress and I play all sorts of people. I play every class, everything and so I feel like that’s what my job is. But think the hard things to read online was when they got really nasty.

I think she’s a well thought out character. She’s got heart. She’s got soul. She cares very much for her baby. She’s got amazing morals. She loves her family to pieces. She would die for them, as you will see. It’s not just one note. There’s more to her than what you see in the trailer. The film is much more layered. I think they probably designed the trailer a little bit to get people talking.

It’s sort of all about that, really.

He’s kind of like a giant kid who’s had too much sugarish. Sometimes it’s like trying to wrangle a hurricane. It’s chaos, but in a wonderful way and I think that shows in the work he makes. It’s just not normal, but it’s exciting, you know, and it’s interesting, and exhilarating and also terrifying. All those things. There’s so much adrenaline going around in your in your body. That’s his gift to you.

I know it’s crazy. I think this will probably be the last one.

article_text:
Del nuevo thriller argentino de Ricardo Darín y Diego Peretti al terror de Evil Dead: En llamas y el regreso de Marvel con VisionQuest , cinco propuestas para disfrutar este fin de semana en streaming.

Las plataformas de streaming renuevan sus catálogos con propuestas para todos los gustos, desde películas argentinas y dramas románticos hasta el terror más sangriento y las nuevas historias del universo Marvel. Este fin de semana, Netflix , Prime Video , HBO Max , Disney+ y Universal+ presentan cinco opciones para quienes buscan algo nuevo para ver desde casa.

En Cinéfilos, repasamos los títulos que vale la pena sumar a la lista, con alternativas para los amantes del cine, las series y las historias que dan que hablar.

Lo dejamos acá – Netflix

Ricardo Darín y Diego Peretti vuelven a compartir pantalla en Lo dejamos acá , una película argentina dirigida por Hernán Goldfrid que combina comedia negra y drama a partir de una relación entre un psicoanalista y su paciente.

La historia sigue a un terapeuta pragmático que comienza a perder la fe en los métodos tradicionales de la psicología y decide cruzar ciertos límites con sus pacientes. Su particular manera de trabajar parece dar resultados hasta que llega a su consultorio un escritor atravesado por un bloqueo creativo, cuya presencia altera una dinámica que parecía funcionar bajo control.

Con un elenco encabezado por Darín y Peretti, junto a Antonia Bengoechea, la producción propone una mirada sobre los límites de la terapia, las contradicciones humanas y las decisiones que pueden tener consecuencias inesperadas.

Para quienes buscan una película nacional con diálogos mordaces, situaciones incómodas y humor oscuro, Lo dejamos acá es una de las opciones destacadas de Netflix para este fin de semana.

El amor de tu vida – Prime Video

El romance y el drama llegan a Prime Video con El amor de tu vida , una película dirigida por Rachel Morrison y protagonizada por Margaret Qualley , Gabriel Basso y Aaron Pierre .

La historia sigue a Maya, una mujer que conoce a Charlie por casualidad y vive con él un romance intenso que parece abrirle las puertas a un futuro con el que siempre soñó. Sin embargo, cuando sus planes se derrumban, debe enfrentarse a una nueva realidad y replantearse quién es, qué desea y cómo volver a amar.

La película explora las relaciones sentimentales, las pérdidas y la posibilidad de reconstruirse después de un cambio inesperado. En lugar de centrarse únicamente en el enamoramiento, la propuesta pone el foco en lo que sucede cuando una historia de amor no sigue el camino imaginado.

Con una trama atravesada por las segundas oportunidades, El amor de tu vida es una alternativa para quienes prefieren los dramas románticos y las historias emocionales.

Evil Dead: En llamas – HBO Max

Los fanáticos del terror tienen una cita con Evil Dead: En llamas , la nueva entrega de la franquicia conocida por su violencia explícita, sus criaturas demoníacas y sus escenas perturbadoras.

Dirigida por Sébastien Vaniček, la película sigue a una mujer que, tras perder a su esposo, busca consuelo junto a sus suegros en una casa familiar aislada. Lo que debería ser un encuentro para atravesar el duelo se transforma rápidamente en una pesadilla cuando los integrantes de la familia comienzan a convertirse en criaturas demoníacas conocidas como Deadites.

A medida que el horror se apodera de la reunión, la protagonista descubre que las promesas realizadas en vida pueden tener consecuencias incluso después de la muerte.

Con Souheila Yacoub, Tandi Wright, Hunter Doohan y Luciane Buchanan entre sus protagonistas, la producción apuesta por el terror sobrenatural y el gore, con una historia que lleva el caos directamente al ámbito familiar.

Si buscás una película intensa, con escenas sangrientas y una atmósfera oscura, Evil Dead: En llamas es una de las alternativas para este fin de semana en HBO Max.

VisionQuest – Disney+

El universo cinematográfico de Marvel continúa expandiéndose con VisionQuest , la serie que completa la trilogía iniciada con WandaVision y continuada con Agatha, ¿quién si no? .

La historia vuelve a centrarse en Visión, el androide reconstruido que intenta encontrar un nuevo propósito después de los acontecimientos que marcaron su existencia. Mientras permanece oculto de quienes pretenden convertirlo en un arma, comienza a explorar su identidad y a buscar respuestas entre las distintas inteligencias artificiales que forman parte de su programación.

Entre ellas se encuentra Ultrón, una presencia que promete complicar todavía más el camino del protagonista. Sin embargo, su aparente tranquilidad se termina cuando una recompensa por su cabeza lo obliga a escapar junto a un misterioso joven que podría estar relacionado con su pasado familiar.

Paul Bettany vuelve a interpretar a Visión, mientras que James Spader retoma su papel como Ultrón. La serie profundiza en cuestiones como la memoria, la identidad y los límites entre la inteligencia artificial y la humanidad.

Para los seguidores de Marvel, VisionQuest representa una oportunidad para reencontrarse con personajes conocidos y descubrir una nueva etapa de una de las historias más particulares del universo de la franquicia.

Crystal Lake – Universal+

El terror también dice presente en Universal+ con Crystal Lake , la serie que amplía el universo de Viernes 13 y explora los orígenes de una de las figuras más reconocidas del cine de terror.

La producción funciona como una precuela de la película original y pone el foco en Pamela Voorhees, la madre de Jason, para indagar en los acontecimientos que anteceden a la historia que convirtió al personaje en un ícono del género.

Interpretada por Linda Cardellini, Pamela ocupa un lugar central en una trama que explora su relación con su hijo y el entorno en el que se desarrolla la historia. A partir de ese vínculo, la serie busca construir una nueva perspectiva sobre los orígenes de la saga y el horror asociado al lago Crystal Lake.

La propuesta está dirigida a quienes disfrutan de las historias de asesinos, los secretos del pasado y las precuelas que recuperan personajes y escenarios emblemáticos.

Con Crystal Lake , los seguidores de Viernes 13 tienen una nueva oportunidad para regresar a uno de los universos más reconocibles del terror y conocer otra parte de su historia.

article_text:
Less than two blocks from the Katonah train station stands a nondescript, gray two-story building on one of the main drags of this Hudson Valley town. Emblazoned in a kerned-out serif font, its name, Branchline, belies what awaits inside: a public-facing exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection (GFC).

Established just five years ago, the GFC has already become one of the world’s leading collections of contemporary Indigenous art, with more than 850 works. Until now, works from the GFC have primarily hung in the New York apartment of Becky Gochman , the collection’s founder and custodian, and her family, though some 200 works are typically on loan to institutions around the world at any given time. The GFC has generously opened the home to museum groups, schools, and artists for tours and events as a way to bring more attention to Native artists, but the organization’s ambition has always been to make its holdings as accessible as possible.

“It’s one thing to articulate a mission, but what matters to me,” GFC creative director and curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít) said Thursday during a press preview, “is if I’m putting that language out into the world [then] I’m making sure that our organization is following that with action.” She added that she sees Branchline as a place for “bringing community together, which means making the Native community feel like they are very much a part of what the decision-making parts of this are, and then also inviting the community of Katonah to come in and learn about new artists that they might not have heard of.”

Anticipating that many visitors will arrive via Metro-North, the GFC named the space after the rail term “branch line,” or the place “where paths diverge and new paths begin,” as GFC director Laura Phipps put it. “We were excited about all the sort of ideas that ‘branch line’ conjures—both thinking about the metaphor of the train and the metaphor of trees—and what we can do to experiment and grow in this space.”

Free to the public, Branchline is taking its time to grow into its new digs, which will eventually total 10,000 square feet across four buildings. Friday evening’s inauguration will show off the first completed space, as well as plans for expansion in the coming months across an L-shaped plot that runs from the main building’s entrance on the Parkway to Katonah Avenue. The building houses a three-room gallery on the ground floor, two bedrooms upstairs for invited artists to determine how they want to spend the time, and a nearly operational ceramics studio downstairs.

Architectural renderings on view Thursday afternoon show that the building’s back door will open onto a small sculpture deck leading to a yet-to-be-built barn, where large-scale works will go on view. (The original barn was in such bad shape that it had to be torn down to make way for an exhibition space.) The barn will in turn lead to the Annex, which will take a more experimental approach (more on that later). From there, visitors will turn left onto a patio and eventually reach the back entrance of Twig, a retail store and café.

For now, visitors will get a taste of Branchline’s ambitions through a more traditional offering. Inaugurating the modest, nearly 2,000-square-foot gallery is “Line Break,” curated by GFC assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee + Diné) with collection associate Nicole van Brugge. “Lines are a core facet of all visual language,” the exhibition’s introductory wall text begins, but Begay and van Brugge look past the formal qualities that a line and its breaks contribute to a work. Instead, they treat the line as a metaphor for lineage and bloodlines, borders and cartographic marks, horizons and sound barriers.

A tight show of 28 works by 18 Indigenous artists, “Line Break” offers visually compelling juxtapositions of artists from different generations working in a range of mediums and styles. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s The Spaniard (1988), a semi-abstract aerial view of the Flathead Indian Reservation in Montana, hangs next to Sara Flores’s Untitled (Shao Pei Maya Kené) , 2024, a painting rendered in the geometric abstract visual language of the Shipibo-Conibo people, whose designs, according to an exhibition brochure, “map the community’s local worldview, environmental understanding, and cosmology.” Farther along are Teresa Baker’s Echoes (2024) and George Morrison’s Night Shadows. Red Rock Variation: Lake Superior Landscape (1994). Both are brightly colored abstract meditations on landscape made in very different mediums: acrylic, yarn, willow, and artificial sinew on AstroTurf for Baker; acrylic on canvas on board for Morrison.

Even the most seemingly formal works reveal their secrets as you delve deeper into how these artists use lines to make meaning. Across from the Quick-to-See Smith and Flores works are two pieces from Nadia Myre’s “Code of Construction” series, in which the artist arranges strung ceramic cylinders into squares depicting the ground-to-air distress signals for “Require Map and Compass” and “Not Understood.” Myre’s choice of medium draws on the tradition of wampum belts, used by Indigenous communities of the Northeast Woodlands to communicate political relationships. Myre’s work finds an analog in Faye HeavyShield’s the red line II (2025), a strand of red beads that the artist strung by hand. Here it is displayed in a coil, though its configuration is flexible—perhaps a metaphor countering the seeming immutability of shape, form, and even time.

The exhibition reaches its crescendo at its center with Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021–24), a handwoven wool textile accompanied by a multichannel sound piece whose low hum visitors have been hearing since entering the gallery. In 2016, Chacon noticed the sounds made by drones flying over the Oceti Sakowin camp at Standing Rock, where protesters had gathered to oppose the Dakota Access Pipeline. Ranging from loud and piercing to soft and soothing, the sounds of police surveillance drones mingled and merged with those of the protesters’ countersurveillance drones. In that harmonious dissonance, Chacon saw a score, which he recorded and also translated into the woven textile, charting the drones’ erratic flight patterns in a traditional Diné weaving style and structure.

Rounding out “Line Break” are two elements that will likely look drastically different in a few months. The GFC commissioned Matthew Kirk to make a site-specific work for an exterior wall of the building along an alleyway. Across three plywood panels, Kirk has collaged painted tar paper in various abstract forms and shapes. The work was already showing its ephemeral quality on Thursday morning, the paper having warped in the light rain.

A few steps down the alleyway is the Annex, which is still under construction: the plywood is exposed, and power cords run to jerry-rigged lightbulbs that illuminate its two floors. Rather than hide this rawness, the GFC team has decided to embrace it. For now, the Annex is home to a small show of drawings by Shuvinai Ashoona, who maps imagined scenes—ones that could perhaps one day come true—onto the Arctic landscape where she lives in Nunavut, Canada. The team acknowledged that it hasn’t quite figured out how the space will look in the near term, even once the build-out is complete. That will depend on how artists interpret a prompt that gives them the autonomy to do what they want.

“What GFC is doing is not trying to become an institution,” Martin said. “It’s trying to just meet where things are needed, and a space is definitely needed for art that is outside of the white box that you’re used to seeing, so that’s what we’re offering.”

Good afternoon, newsletter crew. Welcome back to another edition after a week of geopolitical intrigue plus all the usual news ‘n’ deep dives. Read on. And sign up for the full Insider experience here .

Election Double

“What is behind the door?” Two hugely defining elections saw ballots cast on different sides of the world this week, both of which amass tonnes of interest from the global entertainment industry. The Israeli and Brazilian elections could define a generation in their respective nations. In Brazil , the challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair, a close Donald Trump ally who is currently in prison for plotting a coup, lost narrowly to the incumbent Lula , who landed a fourth term. In Israel , votes are now finally counted , but neither side has a majority. Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc does not have the requisite number of seats, while opposition parties have a majority, but to build a coalition would require challenger Gadi Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, which would represent a turning point in Israeli history. Neither Bolsonaro nor Netanyahu are going quietly. From the U.S., where he has just flown to, Bolsanoro insists he is “leader of Brazil,” while Netanyahu has tasked security services with investigating foreign interference in funding for Arab parties. As regular readers know, Israel and Brazil have always punched well above their weight in the TV and film industry. But in Israel at least, creatives have been stymied in recent years by a plethora of measures that have left them squeezed between censorship at home and international boycotts. On the whole, they are desperate for the Netanyahu era to finally end. “It’s like a horror film because I don’t know what is behind the door,” director Tom Shoval told Melanie just before polls opened in this fascinating deep dive , which is well worth your time. U.S mid-terms are coming (just ask Michael Douglas ) and this week certainly got us election watchers in the mood.

Tokyo Drift

Watch on Deadline

A week of announcements: To Tokyo, where the first week of this year’s Tokyo Film Festival was shaped by big announcements. At the opening ceremony, Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged to boost exports of Japanese content to $127BN by 2033 . Later in the week, Buddy Marini, Amazon MGM Studios’ new head of Japan, said the company has doubled its investment in original Japanese content. The Cannes Marché du Film and Tokyo Film Festival Content Market also revealed they will co-organize the Japan IP Market in Cannes for a second consecutive year , and the Association of Japanese Animations reported that Japan’s anime industry grew by 15.8% to $28.2BN (¥4.45TR) in 2025. So there’s a lot to be happy about in the local market. There will soon even be a new local arthouse distributor in play, thanks to Matt Kelson’s CineYama (pictured above). The ex-Netflix staffer’s interview with Zac is well worth a read. Visitors to the festival this week have included Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences CEO Bill Kramer, who told Deadline that AMPAS will expand the list of festivals that can serve as standalone qualifiers for the International Film Oscar category. Cate Blanchett also joined Shahrbanoo Sadat and Mohammad Rasoulof, two filmmakers who have produced short films under her Displacement Film Fund, for a screening at the festival. Next week, Rasoulof will receive the festival’s Kurosawa award for career achievement before the fest closes on November 4.

The Deadline Interview: Domingo Corral

It came as quite the shock to the international TV and film community when Domingo Corral exited Movistar after more than a decade last year, but Corral isn’t moping. Corral tells Deadline he now sees his production deal with HBO Max as the route to realizing an ambition to make independent TV and film that is both mainstream and premium in quality. “For me, HBO is not just a client; it’s a group of people who share the same vision and very similar sensibilities,” he said. >>> Read The Interview

Global Breakout: ‘Derek vs Derek ‘

We took a rare trip to, drum roll, South West England this week to profile a documentary of warring neighbors that is on the rise. Derek vs Derek started life as a doc about rewilding, but became something quite different when EP Adam Wishart realized one of its protagonists had a rival stationed on the farm opposite him. Neatly for the storyline, they were both called Derek. “There aren’t many documentaries about people like them,” BAFTA-nominee Wishart told Deadline. Now, the movie is attracting more and more bums on seats and next month comes a U.S. festival premiere. >>> Read the Breakout

🌶️ Another : A24’s fantasy epic Elden Ring will become the biggest-budget movie ever sold at a market next month when it heads to the American Film Market.

🧑‍⚖️ Latest from the courtroom: Russell Brand and his wife Laura gave evidence this week as the presenter’s high-profile London trial draws to a conclusion. All coverage here .

🏪 Setting up shop: Phil Hunt is opening a Head Gear Films U.S. hub , with plans to sink $120M into indie film and TV in year one.

🧩 Puzzle complete: The new Skydance international structure was set by JB Perrette , with Andrew Georgiou exiting.

🍳 What’s cooking, Meghan?: You won’t be seeing her in The Gentlemen (yet) but Meghan Markle is instead to co-host Junior MasterChef Australia .

👏 New gig: Ex-Netflix Germany film chief Sasha Bühler has moved to Prime Video to oversee originals in the nation that brought Maxton Hall to the world.

Aperture Celebrates 2026 Gala

The celebration on November 5 honored Deana Lawson and Hiroshi Sugimoto, and was presented by Belmond

Photo by Skylar Searing/BFA.com

Aperture News - November 6, 2026

On Thursday, November 5, Aperture celebrated its 2026 Gala at the American Museum of Natural History, in the heart of the Upper West Side, home to Aperture’s newly opened headquarters at 380 Columbus Avenue in New York City. The evening honored acclaimed photographers Deana Lawson and Hiroshi Sugimoto. The annual benefit, Aperture’s most significant fundraising event of the year, raised over $1 million, providing essential funding that sustains and advances Aperture’s established history of supporting artists and creating landmark publications. The 2026 Aperture Gala was presented by Belmond.

Gala cochairs were Dr. Kathryn Beal, Allan and Anna Chapin, Catherine Gund and Anna Traggio, in memory of Agnes Gund, Dr. Bruce M. Halpryn and Chas Riebe, Lyle Ashton Harris, Arthur Jafa, Judy Glickman Lauder, Lisa Rosenblum and Georgina Celebic, and Thomas R. Schiff and Mary Ellen Goeke. To introduce the esteemed honorees, Sarah Meister saluted Hiroshi Sugimoto, and Dr. Kenneth Montague, Trustee, Aperture, presented Deana Lawson.

Remarking on Sugimoto’s remarkable six-decade career, Meister celebrated how the photographer has “redefined the metaphysical possibilities of the still image,” and noted that it was fitting to “celebrate him in the very museum” where his first photographic series, Dioramas , began.

Dr. Montague then reflected on Lawson’s groundbreaking practice, stating that “Deana’s images are full of love for her community and her subjects radiate with a palpable energy that demands our attention and respect.”

Guests dined beneath the iconic ninety-four-foot-long blue whale model in the Irma and Paul Milstein Family Hall of Ocean Life. As part of the fundraising festivities, a silent auction featured artwork by more than a dozen artists central to Aperture’s publishing history, including Dawoud Bey, Lee Friedlander, and Justine Kurland. A spirited live auction conducted by Christy Coombs, Senior Vice President, Head of Sotheby’s Museum and Corporate Art Group, Americas, featured a gelatin-silver print by Hiroshi Sugimoto; a one-of-a-kind photograph from Richard Learoyd’s Flowers series; an unprecedented opportunity to sit for a commissioned portrait by Tina Barney, whose Fashion monograph (Aperture, 2026) was just released; a journey aboard Belmond’s legendary Venice Simplon-Orient-Express; and a private artist-led tour of Taryn Simon | Father Country I Do Love You on view at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York.

Joining the celebration was a host of artists, curators, and supporters who have collaborated with Aperture on publications and programs over the years, including David Alekhuogie, Tina Barney, Dawoud Bey, Mitch Epstein, Rahim Fortune, E.A. KAHANE, Ethan James Green, Martine Gutierrez, Lyle Ashton Harris, Justine Kurland, An-My Lê, Danny Lyon, Philip Montgomery, Melissa O’Shaughnessy, Anastasia Samoylova, Stephen Shore, Taryn Simon, Coreen Simpson, and Deborah Willis.

Proceeds from the gala and auction sustain Aperture’s work as a nonprofit leader in the field of photography, including its award-winning publications, educational initiatives, touring exhibitions, and public programming. Aperture relies on contributions not only from the gala but also from dedicated readers and enthusiasts, and gratefully accepts donations of any amount through aperture.org/support .

Aperture thanks all of the 2026 Gala supporters, including Aperture Legacy Stars Judy Glickman Lauder and Thomas R. Schiff and Mary Ellen Goeke; Minor White Visionaries Dr. Kathryn Beal, Allan and Anna Chapin, Catherine Gund and Anna Traggio, in memory of Agnes Gund, Dr. Bruce M. Halpryn and Chas Riebe, and Lisa Rosenblum and Georgina Celebic; Dorothea Lange Leaders Mark Gimbel and Dede Welles, Elizabeth and William Kahane, MUUS Collection, and Melissa and James O’Shaughnessy; and Ansel Adams Advocates S. B. Cooper and R. L. Besson, Gregory and Aline Gooding, Terry Hermanson, Ingram Content Group, Cathy M. Kaplan and Renwick D. Martin, Philippe Laumont, Leica Camera, and Dr. Stephen W. Nicholas and Ellen Sargent.

Thanks to those who made the live auction possible, including Sotheby’s, along with Fraenkel Gallery, Gallery Koyanagi, Lisson Gallery, Richard Learoyd, Tina Barney, Belmond, Taryn Simon, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum. Images from the evening are posted on BFA.com .

article_text:
Ulrike Ottinger, die Königin feministischer Pop-Art, ist als Regisseurin zurück. In "Die Blutgräfin" spielt Isabelle Huppert eine nimmersatte Vampirin. Statt Plot gibt es Glamour, Wiener Prachtkulissen und digitales Getier

"Wiener Blut! Eig'ner Saft, voller Kraft, voller Glut!" Man stelle sich vor, die berühmten Zeilen aus Johann Strauss‘ Operette sänge eine Vampirin. Und man stelle sich vor, diese Worte würden keine nette Liebeskomödie begleiten, sondern ein äußerst makabres Festgelage, geöffnete Wiener Kehlen inklusive. Willkommen bei "Die Blutgräfin", dem neuen, opulent ausgestatteten Kinofilm der Regisseurin und Künstlerin Ulrike Ottinger , geschrieben in Zusammenarbeit mit Elfriede Jelinek und gedreht in Wien, der Metropole des Morbiden.

Die Handlung der Horrorkomödie ist schnell erzählt und eigentlich nebensächlich: "Blutgräfin" Erzsébet Báthory (Isabelle Huppert) und ihre treue Gehilfin, die Zofe Hermine (Birgit Minichmayr), sind erzürnt. Ein sagenhaftes Buch soll die Kraft besitzen, ihrem vampirischen Treiben ein Ende zu setzen. Das muss verhindert werden.

Auf ihrer Suche nach dem ominösen Objekt machen die beiden nicht nur die Wiener Hofburg, die Kaffeehäuser und die Kanalisation unsicher, sondern öffnen auch die Kehlen so mancher "Wiener Madeln". Auch nach sechs Jahren Pause von der Leinwand gilt bei Ulrike Ottinger, der Schöpferin feministischer Leinwandexzesse wie "Bildnis einer Trinkerin" oder "Freak Orlando": girls just wanna have fun!

Verweis auf Arcimboldo

Obervampirin Báthory heuert bald auch ihren Neffen Baron Rudi Bubi (Thomas Schubert) an. Der vegetarisch lebende, schüchterne Mann will mit den Blutorgien seiner Familie Báthory aber eigentlich nichts zu tun haben. Lieber nascht er Buchteln im Kaffeehaus Hawelka und sucht dabei Giuseppe Arcimboldos groteske Gemüse-Stillleben nach Botschaften für die Vampirwelt ab.

So sehr Ulrike Ottinger in ihrem neuesten Werk vor allem dem Klamauk huldigt, so sehr finden sich auch ganz ernstgemeinte Rückbezüge auf die Kunst. Beim Gespräch nach der Viennale-Premiere ihres Films in Wien erzählt sie, dass der Verweis auf den Künstler Arcimboldo nicht ganz zufällig sei: Die Bilder ihres Films sollen wie barocke Gemälde wirken, in denen kein Detail, keine Requisite dem Zufall überlassen ist.

Wobei Ottingers Pathos immer mit einem Augenzwinkern kommt. So fliegt durch das gemäldetaugliche winterliche Umland Wiens plötzlich Báthorys computeranimierte Fledermaus Pipistrello. Im mit prächtigen Jugendstilmöbeln ausgestatteten Eingangszimmer eines Hotels schnurrt ein vampirischer Staubsauger.

Das Geheimrezept der Ulrike Ottinger

Das Unzusammenhängende prachtvoll zusammenstellen: Das ist das Geheimrezept Ulrike Ottingers . Bereits in ihrer sehr losen Virginia-Woolf-Adaption "Freak Orlando" (1981) durchkreuzten Männer in Dalmatiner-Kostümen oder "Playboy"-Bunnys das historische Szenario. Was Ottinger mit Oscar Wilde anstellte, verrät bereits der Titel ihres Films "Dorian Gray im Spiegel der Boulevardpresse" (1984). Für die 1942 geborene Ottinger, die als Pop-Art-Künstlerin begann , aber auch fotografierte und bei allen ihren Filmen (bis auf diesen) Kamerafrau war, sind Filme Gesamtkunstwerke.

Das Drehbuch ihrer von der Historie der mörderischen ungarischen Gräfin Elisabeth Báthory (1560–1614) inspirierten "Blutgräfin", so erzählt sie auf der Viennale, war mit Fotografien, Zeichnungen, aber auch Hintergrundinfos zu den Orten so sehr vollgestopft, dass die 84-Jährige es nicht mehr allein tragen konnte.

Ulrike Ottingers Werk steckt voller Bezüge. Schon die erste Einstellung des Films zeigt die in strahlendes Blutrot gekleidete Gräfin durch die Wiener Kanalisation gleiten, auf einem surrealistischen Boot, das eine gigantische Erweiterung ihres Kleids darstellt. Das knallige Rot zitiert "Freak Orlando", in dem Delphine Seyrig ein prachtvolles Lackkleid in dieser Farbe trägt. Die Kostüme für "Die Blutgräfin" entwickelte die Allrounderin zusammen mit dem Chilenen Jorge Jara, der das üppige Barocke ihres Films perfekt verstanden hat – und das Katholische, was für Wien besonders wichtig ist.

Farben so schön wie Blut

Überhaupt Wien: Die morbide Stadt, die nach einem Sprichwort erst 50 Jahre nach der restlichen Welt untergehen wird, ist der ideale Ort für unsterbliche Vampire. In die Christusfarben Rot und Blau gekleidet, streift Isabelle Huppert an atmosphärisch ausgeleuchteten Tourismusattraktionen vorbei, darunter auch die knallig-trashigen Praterkulissen, denen Ottinger 2007 ein Dokumentarfilmdenkmal setzte. Neben Hupperts markanten Outfits, zu denen Accessoires wie ein Füller mit Totenkopf gehören, wirken die anderen Figuren, auch ihr Neffe Baron Rudi Bubi im minzgrünen Blümchenjackett, vampirisch blass. Es muss kaum erwähnt werden, dass Huppert die Rolle als wortwörtlich eiskalte Gräfin bravourös verkörpert, süffisant, charmant und mit der nötigen Abgründigkeit.

Die braucht es aber auch. Ansonsten ist der lose Plot um Figuren mit sprechenden Namen wie Theobastus Bombastus, Nepomuk Nachbiss oder Rudi Bubis Therapeut Theobald Tandem (Lars Eidinger) reichlich klamaukig und erinnert bisweilen an deutsche Blödelkomödien der Marke Otto. Dann aber brechen die verschwenderische Laufzeit, die jeder Prachtkulisse und jedem ästhetischen Überschuss den nötigen Raum gibt, und die leise Melancholie mit jeder Erwartbarkeit.

Wenn schließlich der österreichische ESC-Gewinner Conchita Wurst als bissiger Zeremonienmeister "Rise Like a Phoenix" singt, während er von Vampiren in Militärkostümen flankiert und von einem Sondereinsatzkommando der Polizei angeleuchtet wird, weiß man: Das ist Barock, Camp, Collage, Ottinger. Schön, sie wieder im Kino zu sehen.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/d665488d8efc19bd9fe75d84d012f0e1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "矶田老师独特的视角与绝妙的谈吐。这是一档以通俗易懂的解说揭开历史“真实”与“浪漫”的历史随行采访节目。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本期节目以国际日本文化研究中心（日文研）为舞台。以“从西方看SENGOKU”为主题，特别邀请了因荣获美国艾美奖的热门作品《幕府将军》而负责时代考证的日文研副所长弗雷德里克·克莱恩斯（Frederic Ekreins）教授做客！我们将通过日文研引以为傲的珍贵西洋书籍，解读当时的欧洲人是如何认识并评价织田信长、丰臣秀吉、德川家康等日本战国武将的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从意大利出版的武将列传中位居第一页的秀吉肖像画，到本能寺之变仅4年后便传遍全欧洲的信长灭亡新闻，甚至还有荷兰出版的家康的“情书”！我们将为您呈现通过西方人的目光所看到的战国时代新事实与历史浪漫。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/d3f9c72e5f255877cc63509e14530b76.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/576ac39473247ac61c1be02d59ac11d5.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 节目看点 ①【看点①】与《幕府将军》时代考证者克莱恩斯教授共同解读“世界HERO·秀吉” 在1683年威尼斯出版的《著名武将列传》中，丰臣秀吉竟作为世界98位英雄中的第1位（打头阵）被介绍。头戴帽子的西洋风秀吉画像、过于真实的评价，以及作为“内府大人”被描绘的德川家康的形象等，我们将走近当时的西方对日本的高知名度。 ②本能寺之变后4年！在罗马出版的路易·弗洛伊斯报告书 紧邻本能寺的基督教会（南蛮寺）。从目击事件的传教士卡利昂（Carion）传给路易·弗洛伊斯、再传到欧洲的“信长的末日”。我们将走近被翻译成各欧洲语言并成为畅销书的惊人情报网络真相，以及通往现代的日本情报能力。 ③】描绘的是德川时代的大坂城！？荷兰历史书与“大坂之阵”的误解 在1669年于荷兰出版的历史书中描绘的“大坂夏之阵”插图。仔细观察熊熊燃烧的大坂城，竟然不是丰臣时代的大坂城！？其理由究竟是什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "（美术展Navi编辑部）", "translated": true}]

article_text:
磯田先生のユニークな視点と絶妙な語り口。わかりやすい解説で歴史の『真実』と『ロマン』を解き明かす歴史同行取材番組です。

今回は国際日本文化研究センター（日文研）が舞台です。「西洋から見るSENGOKU」と題し、スペシャルゲストに、米エミー賞受賞の話題作『SHOGUN 将軍』で時代考証を担当した日文研副所長のフレデリック・クレインス教授を迎えます！当時のヨーロッパ人が、織田信長、豊臣秀吉、徳川家康といった日本の戦国武将たちをどのように認識し、評価していたのかを日文研が誇る貴重な西洋書から読み解きます。

イタリアで出版された武将列伝の1ページ目を飾った秀吉の肖像画や、本能寺の変のわずか4年後にヨーロッパ全土へ広まっていた信長滅亡のニュース、さらにはオランダで出版された家康の“ラブレター”まで！西洋人の目を通して見えてくる戦国時代の新事実と歴史ロマンをお送りします。

■ 番組の見どころ ①【見どころ①】『SHOGUN』時代考証・クレインス教授と読み解く「世界のHERO・秀吉」 1683年にベネチアで出版された『著名武将列伝』では、世界の英雄98名の中でなんと1位（トップバッター）として豊臣秀吉が紹介されています。帽子をかぶった西洋風の秀吉像や、リアルすぎる評価、そして「内府様」として描かれた徳川家康の描かれ方など、当時の西洋における日本の知名度の高さに迫ります。 ②本能寺の変から4年！ローマで出版されたルイス・フロイスの報告書 本能寺の目と鼻の先にあったキリスト教会（南蛮寺）。事件を目撃した宣教師カリオンからルイス・フロイスへ、そしてヨーロッパへと伝わった「信長の最期」。西洋各国語に翻訳されベストセラーとなった驚くべき情報ネットワークの真相と、現代に通じる日本の情報力について迫ります。 ③】徳川時代の大坂城が描かれた！？オランダの歴史書と「大坂の陣」の誤解 1669年にオランダで出版された歴史書に描かれた「大坂・夏の陣」の挿絵。炎上する大坂城をよく見ると、なんと豊臣時代の大坂城ではなかった！？その理由とは。

Vo Vo’s Street Meetz (2026) is a VHS-style complication of interviews: trans teenagers at a local amine convention, punks from the rural Midwest at a Halloween party and a theory-minded gallerist ruminating on the spatial politics of protecting half-empty malls. The most compelling local talents in this year’s edition of Converge 45, a multivenue triennial taking place across the city, all harbour a distinct intensity that reflects the interests and character of a city whose sub- cultures and contemporary art communities are only distantly connected to commercial activities in international art metropolises. article_text:
The multivenue triennial leans into creating connection between locals and nonlocals in a rapidly transforming city

At Movie Madness, a Portland institution that preserves the art of the DVD rental, is a dramatic reminder that the city is a liberal haven for misfits. Vo Vo’s Street Meetz (2026) is a VHS-style complication of interviews: trans teenagers at a local amine convention, punks from the rural Midwest at a Halloween party and a theory-minded gallerist ruminating on the spatial politics of protecting half-empty malls. The most compelling local talents in this year’s edition of Converge 45, a multivenue triennial taking place across the city, all harbour a distinct intensity that reflects the interests and character of a city whose sub- cultures and contemporary art communities are only distantly connected to commercial activities in international art metropolises. At Hoffman Gallery at Lewis & Clark College, the indulgent figuration in Srijon Chowdhury’s bloody-hued painting of a woman giving birth next to a doula – as seen in a third woman’s iris – enwraps the scene in an atmosphere of solidarity: birth, a loaded signifier, here binds three women together in pain and renewal. At Center for Contemporary Art and Culture at Pacific Northwest College of Art is Ido Radon’s sarcastically titled Men make their own history… (2026), a sculptural installation of 14 skeletal and unfinished-looking towers arranged on a grid. Radon formally and symbolically cites games like chess, with its modernist, intellectual associations, as well as Erector sets and Chutes and Ladders, which are marketed towards adolescents and preschoolers, respectively – mocking both masculinity and modernist optimism towards the construction of new realities.

Here, To you, Now focuses on Oregon-based artists while bringing in a handful of others from New York, California and abroad. MORE and more (2026), New York-based artist Trisha Baga’s 3D video installation at Portland Institute for Contemporary Art, relays and overlays footage of the artist’s child, computer screen recordings and outer space simulations into a swirling sea of imagery projected against toys. The work considers accumulation as a mode of being and celebrates juvenile potential yet to be dictated or absorbed by larger structures. Read alongside Portland’s growing tech sector, it evokes a rather hopeful comparison between how a child demands nutrition and love and how an LLM demands more training data. Other Spaces (2026), Amy Ruhl’s net.art-looking video installation at Oregon Contemporary, translates Ursula K. Le Guin’s idea of utopias founded on uncertainty into animations of manifesto-writing female androids with campy allusions to failed revolutions, accompanied by sterile, plastic-looking sculptural props that look like they belong in a bio lab. Despite its science fiction framing, the subtext of Ruhl’s rereading of Le Guin speaks most resonantly to the here and now, finding fault in presentist woes like ecological anxiety and political tribalism.

New York-based artist Rose Salane’s exhibition at Cooley Gallery at Reed College, Afterlife in Public , considers magic as a psychic force sitting somewhere between kitsch and parody. In the show’s title work, a multichannel video installation from 2026, a pair of heels worn by Princess Diana and auctioned off to Salane is transformed into a subject and object of this force. Salane commissioned the owner of a small but storied magic shop in Portland, located in a soon-to-be-demolished, beloved mall, to make the shoes appear and disappear before nostalgic and enthralled local audiences. Salane’s videos document the warmly received theatrics, suggesting that a kind of tech-less illusionism can create lasting bonds despite its impermanence. Likewise, Converge 45 seems to lean into creating connection between locals and nonlocals in a rapidly transforming city, resulting in a generative encounter.

article_text:
Fernando Meirelles está al frente de la película que combina un ambicioso robo bancario con traiciones, conflictos personales y un elenco de primer nivel. Llegará a Netflix en enero de 2027.

Dos generaciones de estrellas de Hollywood se cruzan en The Take , la nueva apuesta de Netflix por el cine de suspenso. Denzel Washington y Robert Pattinson encabezan esta producción dirigida por Fernando Meirelles , que acaba de compartir sus primeras imágenes y anticipa una historia en la que nadie parece tener todas las cartas sobre la mesa. Daisy Edgar-Jones , Danai Gurira y Sean Harris completan un reparto que promete ser uno de los grandes atractivos del proyecto.

La película, que durante su desarrollo llevó el título Here Comes the Flood , propone un escenario conocido dentro del género: un robo a gran escala. Sin embargo, su principal apuesta está en cómo contar esa historia. En lugar de ofrecer una visión general de los acontecimientos, el relato seguirá exclusivamente a uno de sus protagonistas, una decisión que permitirá que el misterio acompañe al espectador durante toda la película.

Un robo bancario, tres protagonistas y demasiados secretos

Robert Pattinson interpreta a Noah, un exmilitar que todavía intenta encontrar su lugar fuera del Ejército. Su vida cambia cuando aparece Christian Carter, un delincuente interpretado por Denzel Washington que lo incorpora a un plan para asaltar una importante entidad bancaria de Manhattan.

El golpe, que en principio podría parecer una operación cuidadosamente organizada, adquiere otra dimensión cuando Noah descubre que Rose, su pareja —interpretada por Daisy Edgar-Jones— trabaja precisamente en el banco elegido como objetivo. Así, el protagonista queda atrapado entre una operación criminal y sus propios vínculos personales.

La particularidad narrativa de The Take será que todo estará contado desde los ojos de Noah. El público no tendrá acceso a información que el personaje desconozca, por lo que cada descubrimiento podrá modificar la interpretación de lo sucedido. En ese juego de perspectivas, las apariencias y las verdaderas motivaciones de cada integrante del plan serán fundamentales.

Fernando Meirelles vuelve a Netflix con un elenco de lujo

Detrás de cámaras se encuentra Fernando Meirelles, el realizador brasileño que alcanzó reconocimiento internacional con Ciudad de Dios y que ya trabajó para Netflix en Los dos papas . En esta oportunidad, tendrá a su disposición un reparto encabezado por Washington y Pattinson, acompañado por Daisy Edgar-Jones, Danai Gurira, Sean Harris, Moisés Arias y Justin Kirk.

El guion lleva la firma de Simon Kinberg, responsable de trabajos como X-Men: Días del futuro pasado y Sr. y Sra. Smith . El equipo creativo también incluye a Audrey Chon en la producción.

Los personajes centrales estarán construidos sobre personalidades muy diferentes. Christian es un hombre que confía plenamente en su capacidad para manipular a los demás, mientras que Noah tiene dificultades para confiar, aunque tampoco está exento de ocultar sus propias intenciones. Esa combinación será clave para sostener la tensión de una historia en la que el dinero podría no ser el verdadero objetivo.

¿Cuándo se estrena en Netflix?

The Take tiene previsto su estreno el 15 de enero de 2027 en cines seleccionados y en la N roja. Por ahora, la plataforma no presentó un tráiler completo, pero las primeras imágenes y las declaraciones del reparto ya ofrecen un adelanto de su propuesta.

Con el encuentro entre Denzel Washington, Robert Pattinson y Fernando Meirelles, la película se perfila como uno de los próximos grandes estrenos de suspenso de Netflix. Una historia de atracos, engaños y secretos que promete mantener al público atento hasta su desenlace.

解説・あらすじ

ミステリー作家の藤石波矢と辻堂ゆめがリレー形式で競作した2019年刊行の長編小説「昨夜は殺れたかも」を映画化したラブサスペンス。ダンス＆ボーカルグループ「THE RAMPAGE」のメンバーで「遺書、公開。」など俳優としても活躍する吉野北人と、歌手活動に加えドラマや映画、バラエティー番組にも出演する鈴木愛理が初共演し、互いの正体を隠したまま結婚した夫婦が勘違いから殺し合いを繰り広げる様子を描き出す。 ハロウィンの夜に運命的な出会いを果たした光弘と咲奈。それぞれ平凡な会社員のふりをしたものの、実は光弘の正体はヤクザで、咲奈の正体は若くして起業した敏腕社長だった。やがて結婚した2人は互いに素性を明かさないまま、幸せな夫婦生活を送っていた。しかし、それぞれが浮気をしていると勘違いしたことから、互いの殺害計画を企てるようになっていく。 咲奈が経営する会社の副社長・明石を工藤阿須加、咲奈をサポートする秘書・黒沢を佐津川愛美、光弘が勤める会社の事務員・野中を王林、光弘の会社の社長・梶谷を本宮泰風が演じ、ISSEI、田中美久、オラキオ、河本準一（次長課長）、菅田俊が共演。テレビドラマやドキュメンタリー番組を数多く手がけてきた松木創監督がメガホンをとり、「事故物件 恐い間取り」のブラジリィー・アン・山田が脚本を担当。

article_text:
At 80, Kazakhstan’s pioneer of tapestry looks back on over half a century at the loom – and admits she always wanted to be a painter.

For an artist celebrated as a founder of the Kazakh school of tapestry, Batima Zaurbekova makes a disarming confession. “I always dreamed of being a painter,” she tells me, a few steps from the more than 80 works assembled for her 80th birthday at Almaty’s Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts of the Republic of Kazakhstan . Her teachers at the Alma-Ata Art School, from which she graduated in 1969, warned her off the loom: “They told me, don’t do tapestry, it takes so much time. In the time it takes to make one tapestry, you could make ten paintings.” She did it anyway – working in dense Gobelin, woven on a vertical loom – influenced by a village childhood among flat-woven carpets and by her mother, Bibikhan, a seamstress who sewed national costume. What carries across both disciplines, she suggests, is an instinct for colour. “Everyone can learn to draw,” she says, “but to see colours, to understand them, that is something given to you by God.”

Threads of Heritage , curated by Alina Fedorovich with Natalya Bazhenova, head of the museum’s department of Kazakh decorative and applied arts, makes that pull between brush and thread one of its themes. Several images appear twice, as an oil and as a tapestry – Still Life (1978), which depicts a fruit-laden table among them – so that you can watch a composition migrate from canvas to loom. Around that table, the yurt interior dissolves into contrasting planes of colour and rhythmic lines, closer to stained glass than to felt, so that the domestic space seems almost to sound. It is typical of an artist whose tapestries are conceived in dialogue with lived space – the yurt, the carpet, the curtain – and whose compositions have the flavour of musical improvisations.

The title is apt. For Zaurbekova, it gathers up “our past, our way of life, our history” – a summary, she says, of all of it. Bazhenova reads it more literally. Thread is both the raw material of tapestry and its result, she points out, and each strand stands for a single life: “Each thread represents a person’s life. Each person threads their own life, their own art, into it – and this is the foundation of everything.” The weave itself, as she describes it, forms a cross – a vertical of spirit meeting a horizontal of material life – and from that crossing the whole fabric grows. It is a fitting frame for an artist whose work has always been about continuity: between generations, between craft and art, between the yurt and the museum wall.

The show unfolds across three halls of a museum whose Soviet-era architecture feels a world away from the sleek Almaty Museum of Arts that opened across town last year, to which I owed my last visit to the city. In the first hall, beneath an atrium, a pavilion built for the occasion evokes the Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi in Turkestan, with footage of Zaurbekova’s weaving projected on to its walls. The choice speaks volumes to local visitors: commissioned by Timur in 1389 to honour the twelfth-century Sufi poet whose Turkic-language teachings helped carry Islam across the steppe, the turquoise-domed shrine – never finished, and a Unesco World Heritage Site since 2003 – is Kazakhstan’s foremost place of pilgrimage and a touchstone of national identity. It recurs throughout Zaurbekova’s oeuvre, most notably in a 1990s series devoted to Turkestan and the Silk Road, made as the newly independent country set about reclaiming its past.

Around the edges of the room, the museum’s permanent displays of felt and pile carpets, leather goods, carved wood and ceramics set her tapestries in conversation with the folk objects that fed them. Quraqs (2015), Bazhenova explains, takes its name from the patchwork quilts her mother made. Woven into its patchwork are symbols drawn from ancient petroglyphs, among them the arkhar, the wild mountain sheep that Bazhenova calls a calling card of Kazakhstan. Zaurbekova’s compositions never drift far from traditional Kazakh ornament or from the cultural memory it carries. Ornamental Rug , made in 1969, the year of her graduation and first solo exhibition, is the earliest work on show – and her newest sits not far away.

The second hall is given over to the works themselves, grouped thematically in an open plan. The hang is varied – some pieces framed, some suspended against a backdrop of warp threads, as if still on the loom – and several, including Madonna of the Steppe (1980), can be viewed from both sides. The latter is a highlight: a woman in Kazakh dress distilled into a vertical structure somewhere between an arch and an inverted dome, her outstretched ‘wings’ opening like a cup, the whole suggestive of a Tree of Life. Threads left trailing beyond the tapestry’s edge give it a deliberate air of incompletion, as though the form were still growing. Mountains recur across this gallery, a legacy of Zaurbekova’s birthplace, Merke, alongside cityscapes of Astana and Almaty. Bazhenova points out an undulating line that ripples through many compositions like a sound wave; in her youth, Zaurbekova played the bayan (a kind of accordion).

One work whose title piqued my interest was Kazakhstan (1977). A yurt, sheaves of wheat, figures bound together in shared labour: this is harvest iconography, its colours muted because, Bazhenova explains, artists then drew their yarn from the state carpet factory. Did Zaurbekova feel pressure to tone down her Kazakh subject matter? “No,” she says. “I was free to do whatever I wanted.” The only obligations were thematic exhibitions – Mother Earth , she recalls, was made for an anniversary of the republic. Her real influences lay elsewhere. “I did not like Soviet realism,” she says; before sitting down to work, she would leaf through her books of the Impressionists.

Bazhenova offers a more nuanced view. “The spirit of socialism is present in almost all of the works of that time – it was the spirit of the time,” she explains, while insisting that “there was no pressure on the artist”. Their answers gave me pause for thought. After the terror of the Stalin years – forced collectivisation, the execution of the Alash Orda intellectuals – Soviet pressure on Kazakh culture became quieter but no less persistent: a bureaucratic campaign of Russification under which national cultures were tolerated chiefly in a folkloric register. Tapestry, rooted in craft and ornament, may simply have been the kind of national expression the system found least threatening – a question that the exhibition might have done well to explore.

Where Zaurbekova does describe hardship is after 1991. “Everything disappeared,” she says. The Ministry of Culture stopped buying, the art factory that had supplied commissions shut down, and the artists’ union fund closed. She kept working regardless, building a collection nobody was purchasing. Something of a rescue came in 1997, when a Turkish businessman invited her to Istanbul to teach tapestry, a medium barely known there. Ironically, it was in Türkiye that she finally became a painter, producing 35 landscapes in a month for an exhibition; seven had sold before it even opened. “They had 120 galleries,” she marvels. “We didn’t have any here.” The sea – something else absent from Kazakhstan – entered her work too, in tapestries such as Gifts of the Sea (2004).

The final hall turns to womanhood. A shanyrak, the crown of the yurt and a fixed feature of the building that the designers have turned to their advantage, hovers above portraits of women in the saukele bridal headdress and the kimeshek worn by married women. Alongside are archival photographs, a documentary shot in the late 1970s over a month at the artist’s home and at her mother’s, and a loom on which a weaver periodically sits and demonstrates the craft. Here the interpretation thins: the film and photographs come with little context, a shame given how much story they hold.

The show’s real coda, I feel, lies back in the first hall, in Transitional Season (2026), that newest work, in felt and appliqué, which Bazhenova tells me was started only weeks before the doors opened. Its place beside the museum’s old felts distils the whole exhibition: an 80-year-old artist still returning to, and building on, the folk forms she grew up with.

Asked what she would tell young artists navigating the digital age, Zaurbekova is disarmingly candid. “If AI makes everything, what are we going to do?” she asks. “I don’t understand it myself.” Threads of Heritage offers something of an answer: a loom, worked slowly, thread by thread.

Threads of Heritage runs until 8 November 2026

article_text:
The second round of the Matca Creation Grant supports the production of one photography exhibition and one series of texts, addressing the ongoing lack of sustained support for the professional development of photography practitioners. The exhibition grant is open to Vietnamese nationals residing in Vietnam, while the writing grant welcomes applicants of all nationalities.

We would like to thank everyone who took the time to apply to our open call. After a thorough review process conducted in collaboration with our guest mentors, we are pleased to announce the recipients: Nguyễn Ngọc Hải (Đà Nẵng) for the Exhibition category, and TN Đan (Singapore / HCMC) for the Writing category.

Each recipient will receive 10,000,000 VND to realize their proposals, along with artistic and logistical support from Matca and guest mentors Trương Quế Chi and Zhuang Wubin.

Nguyễn Ngọc Hải (Đà Nẵng) – Recipient of the Exhibition category

Nguyễn Ngọc Hải began shooting film photography in 2018. He currently works as a freelance wedding photographer and occasionally as a BTS photographer for independent films. His personal projects are centered on people from his everyday life, as a means of expressing how he sees and relates to the world. He is largely self-taught, having learned photography through practical experience and short workshops.

Hải will receive 10,000,000 VND and mentorship from artist, curator Trương Quế Chi to realize a solo exhibition at Matca Space for Photography.

TN Đan (Singapore / HCMC) – Recipient of the Writing category

Based in Singapore, TN Đan writes about the visual cultures of Southeast Asia and its representations. His work has appeared in Art&Market, SGIFF, PR&TA, and Matca. He co-runs Monsoon Review, an online site dedicated to examining contemporary and historical production of cultures in Southeast Asia and beyond.

Đan will receive 10,000,000 VND and mentorship from writer, researcher Zhuang Wubin to realize a series of texts in English and Vietnamese.

The Matca Creation Grant is an initiative by Matca that supports photography projects from Vietnam’s local community. The grant provides cash funding, as well as artistic and logistical support, for proposals that involve image-making, writing, and exhibiting photography.

江戸東京博物館（東京都墨田区）で、「日米交流 知のかけはし ―ラトガース・カレッジと幕末明治の日本人留学生―」が10月24日から開催されます。

アメリカ合衆国ニュージャージー州ニューブランズウィック市にあるラトガース・カレッジ（現ニュージャージー州立ラトガース大学）は、1766年に創立したアメリカの中で最も古い歴史を持つ大学の一つです。19世紀後半、日本が近代化へ移行する幕末から明治期にかけて、同大学は数多くの日本人留学生を受け入れました。同大学及び付属のグラマースクール（中等学校）で学んだ留学生たちは、ここを足場にして自分の進路を選択し、それぞれの分野で近代日本の建設を担いました。また、ラトガース出身のアメリカ人もお雇い教師として来日し、明治の教育に多大な貢献をしました。ラトガースと日本人留学生との交流は、日米関係の黎明期を語る上で特筆すべき一ページです。

2026年は、アメリカ合衆国建国250周年の佳節を迎え、またラトガース出身で福井藩及び大学南校の教師として招聘されたウィリアム・エリオット・グリフィスの二度目の来日から100年にあたります。本展では、幕末から明治前期にアメリカへ渡った留学生と教師たちの交流に視点を置き、東京都江戸東京博物館所蔵資料を中心にした展示によって、黎明期における日米交流史が描かれます。

企画展「日米交流 知のかけはし ―ラトガース・カレッジと幕末明治の日本人留学生―」

会場：江戸東京博物館 常設展示室内 5階企画展示室（東京都墨田区横網1-4-1）

会期：2026年10月24日（土）～12月6日（日） ※会期中展示替を行います （前期展示：10/24～11/15、後期展示：11/17～12/06）

開館時間：9:30～17:30（土曜日は19:30まで） ※入館は閉館の30分前まで ※11/6・13・20・27の金曜日はオータムナイトミュージアムにつき20:00まで開館

休館日：10/26、11/4、9、16、24、30

観覧料：常設展観覧料で観覧可能 一般800円 ・65歳以上400円 ・大学生、専門学校生480円・高校生300円 ※中学生以下無料 ※11/6・13・20・27は17:00以降の入館で学生無料（年齢を証明できるものを要提示） ※その他常設展観覧料の免除または割引については同館公式ウェブサイトを参照

詳細は、 東京都江戸東京博物館公式サイト まで。

展示構成

◇プロローグ 開国と英学需要の高まり ◇第1章 高濤遥かに ―勝小鹿の米国留学― ◇第2章 日本人留学生が集う街・ニューブランズウィック ◇第3章 教え子たちの故郷・日本へ ―グリフィスとクラーク― ◇第4章 明治の教育制度と学監マレー ◇エピローグ 日米交流は時を超えて ※本展では、ラトガース大学グリフィスコレクションの実資料展示は行われません。

主な展示資料

出品点数は約80点。ラトガースと日本人留学生との交流を示す資料群を中心に、幕末から明治期にかけての日本の留学生の動向を物語る文物、文化財などが紹介されます。

アメリカ合衆国建国250周年、そしてウィリアム・エリオット・グリフィスの再来日から100年という節目を迎える2026年。激動の幕末から明治初期にかけて、海を越えて学問に情熱を燃やした日本人留学生たちと、海を渡って日本の近代教育の礎を築いたアメリカ人教師たちの絆は、今なお色褪せない輝きを放っています。勝海舟自筆の書をはじめ、当時の熱気をリアルに伝える約80点もの貴重な資料を通じて、知られざる草創期の日米交流の軌跡を追体験できる絶好の機会です。新たな時代の扉を開こうと志を抱いた若者たちの息吹に触れに、ぜひ会場へ足を運んでみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）
